I wish only to endorse the principle of the bill. The minister gave a very fine and detailed description of the aims and objects of this particular agreement. We are now dealing with the short title. I support the bill because I understood the other evening that the resolution was to be adopted. I hope that this bill will be passed by six o'clock. The main point which appeals to the opposition, although I cannot speak for the opposition, is that this bill is giving aid to the mother country. The hon. member for Temiscouata the other night took occasion to tell the opposition a few things, but he forgot that the opposition has adopted the principle of this loan to the mother country.
I have always had a great deal of sympathy with the Minister of Finance for his sincerity of purpose and his ability for hard work, but
I think the finest remark he made was that this lo'an is not charity but an investment with our best customer with whom we want to trade. In the years to come I think it will redound to the credit of the present Minister of Finance and those associated with him in making this agreement. I cannot go so far with him in what he said about other matters in connection with this bill, about the Bretton Woods agreement, for instance, and the Anglo-American loan. The minister said he hoped that these three together would lead to a better world and all that kind of thing, and that a body would be set up by the United States to deal with international trade balances. I have never been a believer in these new worlds to come after the war and all their blueprints. They were to come also after the last war.
So far as this loan to the United Kingdom is concerned, she is our best customer. She has never defaulted. She has invested, not millions, but billions of dollars in this country before we were able to take care of ourselves. Therefore, apart altogether from any sentimental feeling, this loan is good business. Look at the amount of money which Great Britain invested in public works in this country in days gone by, on the Rideau canal, for instance, right here running past the Chateau Laurier. That is only one of the large public works in which Britain invested, millions of dollars in this country. In the same way, after the war between the north and the south in the United States, Great Britain invested millions in the eastern and central States to help them build their state and municipal institutions, their public works, and their railway systems. Consequently this loan is in no sense charity but a good business investment because we are dealing with a country that always meets its obligations.
Something has been said by one of our speakers on this side about Lord Keynes, who was called the greatest economist of our time. He started this Bretton Woods scheme; it was an idea of his, and the Minister of Finance and others here and in London and Washington have told us that this loan is interlocked with Bretton Woods and the Anglo-American loan. But Lord Keynes' idea was not carried out in the final act of Bretton Woods. It was an amendment to his idea. Lord Keynes will not be called a great economist twenty-five years from now, because I remember reading a book that he wrote when I first entered parliament in which he expressed views directly the opposite of those he expressed on the Bretton Woods agreement, the success of which is very doubtful, tied up as it is with
Loan to United Kingdom

the abolition or curtailment of preferences and other impossible conditions. I look on the United States loan to Britain as one of the most unfortuiate things in the history of international finance. It will lead) to untold disputes between the United States and Britain and it imposes the harshest terms that I ever heard of. It is worse than the treatment in terms that Germany got after the last war, treatment which she properly deserved.
I should have liked to see the government go further and get all the dominions, Canada, New Zealand and Australia, to shoulder this Anglo-American total loan together. One of the great mistakes that we made in the war was to surrender too much of our political, financial, economic and military power to Washington. That is where we made a great mistake.
But this particular loan dealt with in bill No. 28 stands on its own feet as a good business investment for Canada to make, and will make for employment in Canada. There are, as the Minister of Finance said, other matters interlocked with it. I want to say this of the Bretton Woods agreement and the Anglo-American loan, that they mean the end of preferential trade within the empire. I know one of our hon. members said that nature has placed us on the North American continent, but that is what they said between the two wars. We would hear people asking why we should depend upon Great- Britain, upon London and Glasgow for defence, and they wanted to reduce the estimates for defence and have us depend on Washington; but I say that Britain and1 the dominions are an economic unit and if we developed preferential trade between the empire we should be far superior to Russia and the United States as an economic power. Let us start this brave new world we are talking about by building a strong economic unit within the empire itself. We know from past experience what preferential trade means. It increased Britain's trade with Canada by 42 per cent and Canada's trade with Britain by 44 per cent, and as well increased international trade by leaps and bounds. We have had in the past this new internationalism in the favoured nation treaties with many foreign countries, but we find that over 84 per cent of all our business was done with the mother country and the United States and only 16 per cent with foreign countries. We have tried this international racket and these dreams of a new world to come before. I have no confidence in it; I do not believe in it. We should stick together within the empire as an economic unit. If we do not hang together we shall hang separately, for none of our dominions
fMr. Church.]
are able to "go it" alone, and Britain without the dominions will be only a second-class power.
There are many things to consider about the Bretton Woods agreement. It is not a scheme of governments but a scheme of economists. I do not believe that it will do what we are told it will. Under it, economic sanctions, if any of us fail, can be applied against Britain and the other dominions; do not forget that. It is only a half-baked international currency scheme which will lead to trouble between Britain and the United States. It is only a half-baked international currency bill, which can never work.
We want full employment-, as far as possible. We want cheap money and stable prices. But we shall never get them under the Bretton Woods, Anglo-American loan. I stand by the Ottawa agreements and empire trade first, but they should be brought up to date, so as to meet changed conditions. United with the other dominions we are strong; divided we shall fall. We. are not strong enough for any of us to go alone.
I believe the present government, and those which have preceded it, men who held office in the days of Laurier and Fielding, deserve great credit for their pioneering in the matter of preferential trade, and for giving us the six-cent preference on wheat-which was afterwards revoked in 1938 by the. United States treaty. But they were the pioneers.
Do not throw it all to the wolves for the sake of a so-called new thing, this dream of a new world, called internationalism. As I have said, the final word of the Bretton Woods agreement is not found in this plan. The final act has been changed, from first to last. They would have Great Britain throw away the only real assets she has, namely her purchasing power in her own home market. She will have to trade that way, and without these two loans will have to regulate and control her export trade and imports. Through the development of consolidation within the empire, Great Britain can build up an economic unit, pledge full employment, and raise the standard of living. All that will be killed by the Bretton Woods agreement. It brings us back to the laissez-faire doctrine of the twenties and the thirties, to -the status quo of 1929 and 1939. I want an economic system which, in the circumstances of 1944, 1945 and 1946 or 1960 can help mankind toward a goal of increasing production. The Bretton Woods scheme and the Anglo-American loan will hand over world economic power, and with it world domination, because of the $28 billion of gold in the world, $23 billion are held by the United States.

Loan to United Kingdom
Great Britain cannot recover unless she is permitted to assume her place in the trade of the world. This trade is not exclusive. The Bretton Woods agreement and the United States loan do not constitute an exchange of goods and services for an exchange of goods and services. It has to be paid back some time, with interest. The United States loan is an exchange of gools and services for what? It is for debt, or for gold. I believe the conditions of the Anglo-American loan are very harsh and a surrender to the money-lenders who do not consider the money was spent to save their shores from invasion for over two years.
If anyone believes the United States will have lower tariffs, then just let him read the recent record's of the senate and house of representatives in Washington. There will always be tariffs, so long as there are countries. There will always be nations, and patriotism is the cement that holds nations together. For us to blind our eyes to all this, and go roaming around the world looking for brave new worlds and international agreements is something beyond belief.
In conclusion, let me refer to the speech made this afternoon by an hon. member who spoke first, and who is not at the moment in his seat. He is a fluent, most informative and interesting speaker. But he has forgotten some of the figures, which are set out in a table issued from Washington which shows the principal international credits or loans, either extended or awaiting approval to France by Canada and the United States. This publication is by the National City Bank of New York, April issue, dealing with the subjects of economic conditions, governmental finance and United States securities. At page 44 there is a review of what was done at Savannah recently regarding Bretton Woods. They found that they will have to mark time, and do something. This is what is stated'.
There is general approval of the apparent trend toward postponing starting the monetary fund until some time after the international bank begins operations. This is what many people have advocated all along, for successful operation of the fund is possible only in a reasonably stable world.
I refer now to the table which shows the credits given or to be sanctioned. The amount extended to Great Britain by the United States is $660 million, while that extended by Canada is given as $1,136 million. The credit extended to France by the United States is $895 million, and by Canada, $220 million. The other figures are given for other countries.
In this connection may I point out to hon. members from the province of Quebec what
was said by the new Prime Minister of France, Felix Gouin, who is a socialist. This is what he said when taking over from General de Gaulle:
France has always reacted with the marvellous power which belongs to her and which is made up of moderation, reason and profound political wisdom.
Everybody hopes that under the loan the minister has made available to France-and it will reflect to his credit in years to come, in the minds of the French-speaking people of Quebec-France will soon thus be able to rebuild accordingly. She is in great need of financial assistance at the present time. Her civil and war expenses are much greater than they should be, and will have to be reduced. However, it is our hope that she will get past this critical time. Canada's loan will help greatly. Everything she needs will be made available to her . from the people of this country, under the loan announced by the Minister of Finance. I believe the minister deserves the thanks of the country for this transaction, although I would qualify my remarks by making the references I did to the Bretton Woods agreement and the Anglo-American agreement, and the cause and effect of it. I do this because I am a real believer in the future policy of Great Britain and her dominions for imperial preference as an economic unit along the lines I have suggested. Under an empire system we would have preferential trade; the Ottawa agreements could be brought up to date, to meet changed conditions.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Acadia asked me a question about the chances of the United States and Canada pursuing a liberal trade policy in the future. I said I thought Lord Keynes, in a speech delivered in the House of Lords, had made reference to the prospects of such a policy being followed in the United States. I now have excerpts from that speech which I believe are worthy of a place on the record.
This is what he is reported to have said at page 791 of the debates of the House of Lords for December 18, 1945:
Questions have been raised-and rightly anil reasonably raised-about the willingness of the United States to receive repayment hereafter. This is a large subject to which I have given a great deal of thought, but I shall not have time to develop it fully to-day. I am not, as a result, quite so worried as most people. Indeed, if nr the next five or ten years the dollar turns out to be a scarce currency, seldom will so many people have been right. It is a very technical matter, very emphatically within their past experience, but not so easily the subject of future prediction. I am afraid I must content myself with a few headlines. First, it is not a question of our having to pay the United States by direct
Loan to United. Kingdom

exports; we could never do that. Our exports are not, and are not likely to be as large as our direct imports from the United States. The object of the multilateral system is to enable us to pay the United States by exporting to any part of the world and it is partly for that very reason that the Americans have felt the multi-laterial system was the only sound basis for any arrangement of this kind. Secondly, all the most responsible people in the United States, and particularly in the state department and in the treasury, have entirely departed from the high tariff, export subsidy conception of things, and will do their utmost with, they beileve. the support of public opinion in the opposite direction. That is why this intternational trade convention presents us with such a tremendous opportunity. For the first time in modern history the United States is going to exert its full, powerful influence in the direction of reduction of tariffs, not only of itself but by all others.
Thirdly, this is a problem of which to-day every economist and publicist in the United States is acutely conscious. Books on economics are scarcely written about anything else. They would regard it as their fault and not ours if they fail to solve it. They would acquit us of blame-quite different from the atmosphere of ten or twenty years ago. They will consider it their business to find a way out. Fourthly, if the problem does arise, it will be a problem, for reasons I have just mentioned, of the United States vis-a-vis the rest of the world and not us in particular. It will be the problem of the United States and the whole commercial and financial arrangement of every other country. Fifthly,-and perhaps this is the consideration which' is least prominent in peoples' minds- the United States is rapidly becoming a high-living and a high-cost country. Their wages are two and a half times ours. These are the historic, classical methods by which in the long run international equilibrium will be restored.
With regard to the questions put to me by the hon. member for Temiscouata, perhaps I should give them a little more thought and answer them at eight o'clock. I could start on them now, perhaps, but I would like to discuss them. Perhaps I shall have to ask him to repeat some of the questions, as I have not notes of all; but following the notes I have here, perhaps I can deal with them.
There is one point I wish to make clear, which I tried to make clear the other day. I referred to Great Britain getting back into a state of equilibrium, and the hon. member said, "What about Canada getting back into equilibrium?" The point I wanted to make was that when I was talking about deficits and about equilibrium I was not talking about an internal situation at all. When I said the United Kingdom went back, or that the United Kingdom's financial position deteriorated by $20,000 million in Canadian funds up to the time of these loans, I was not talking about the internal debt of the United Kingdom, how much the internal debt was or how much it had increased. The internal debt of the United Kingdom is over $100,000 million, so that we are not comparing likes

when we compare an external position with the internal position of the Dominion of Canada. What I meant was that as a result of the war, by loss of foreign assets, by loss of liquid reserves and by debts incurred to foreign countries, the United1 Kingdom had gone back, had worsened its position by an amount equivalent to $20,000 million in. Canadian funds.
The Dominion of Canada did not do that at all. As a result of the war the Dominion of Canada slightly bettered1 its external position. It incurred a large internal debt, but on balance it lessened its external debt. The same applied to the United States of America; I think the same applied to every other one of our allies. The United Kingdom alone among the victorious allies suffered this terrific deterioration in its external position as far as foreign indebtedness, foreign assets, foreign currencies and liquid reserves were concerned. That is why I said in my speech that the case of the United Kingdom is unique, a special case. That was not an expression of sentiment, or something coming from an imperialist. I was saying simply, and almost in the same words, what was said in the United States of America by the national advisory council, consisting of the secretary of the treasury, the under-secretary of state and so on. They recognized the fact, which cannot be escaped, that the United Kingdom case is different from the case of any other country in the world. The United Kingdom occupies a key position. Either we must write it off and say that it is hopeless, that the place is bankrupt and we might as well forget them; or we have to take the other line and do what we reasonably can, within our resources, to get them into a position where they can carry on as they have in the past, as a great trading nation.
Perhaps I am emphasizing the currency end of this a little more than the trade end of it, but the main reason I desire to see this loan go through is that I want sterling once more to be real money, instead of a currency which is not convertible into other currencies. When I was young, and in fact all during the previous war, when we sold goods to Great Britain for sterling that sterling could be converted into United States dollars; not, as during the last war, simply sold by the Canadian exporter to the government of Canada, which could not do anything more with it unless it made some arrangement with the United Kingdom. So that we must get sterling back to the position of convertibility; and the success of these North American loans, the one from the United States and the one from Canada, is necessary if sterling

Judges Act
is to 'become a stable and convertible currency once more. Unless it is, we cannot carry on ths huge trade that we have carried on with Great Britain and upon which our wheat exporters, our bacon exporters, our cheese exporters, our apple exporters, our metals exporters, and so on, absolutely depend. We shall not be able to carry that on; we shall have to reorient ourselves entirely, change our economy completely, reduce our exports enormously and try to make ourselves over into some kind of self-sufficient nation.
Great Britain can very well take that other line. She has an area there, the sterling area. By living within that area and pursuing very restrictive trade policies, not buying from any country unless that country will buy from it, by making these bilateral trade * agreements they can, and in order to live would have to, do these things, being in the position they are in, unless the North American nations show a little imagination and do something to get Great Britain into the position where in future she can carry on the kind of trade policies which are essential to the interests of the Dominion of Canada.
The hon. member for Temiscouata is entirely wrong when he said my eyes were on Great Britain all the time during my speech. I made the speech from the point of view of the Dominion of Canada. I agree with the approach of the leader of the C.C.F. party and the approach of the financial critic of the the opposition. I disagree with the approach of the Social Credit party, because I do not think the Social Credit party is right in the position it takes that this is purely a moral obligation and not a good business proposition. That is based upon a short-run view.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED
speechtext: I do not suppose the minister would remember when I spoke, but he may recall that I did not follow that line, so that perhaps he should be a little less sweeping in his denunciation.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED
speechtext: Your case was like that of England; it was unique.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED
speechtext:
I accept the statement of the hon. member for Lethbridge. Perhaps the members of the Social Credit party were speaking individually, each expressing his own opinion. But while quite a bit of what the hon. member for Acadia says is true, namely that this has an inflationary influence, that it is taking goods out of the country at a time when they are in short supply here, and that goods may be coming back at a time when they are not in short supply here, nevertheless these disadvantages are all outweighed by the paramount advantage of getting Great Britain in a position, not during
the next two or three years but in the next half century, where the United Kingdom will be a trading nation with a stable, convertible currency, taking large quantities of our goods and sending us back goods and currency that we can use to buy goods from the United States and other countries. Therefore, from that point of view, we regard this loan as highly in the interests of thd Dominion of Canada.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: JUDGES NOT TO ACT AS COMMISSIONERS OR ARBITRATORS-TO BE BOUND BY DECISION OF COURT OF FINAL APPEAL

speechtext:
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of bill No. 13, to amend the Judges Act.
He said: I do not wish to delay the minister in getting along with the matter which was under discussion before six o'clock, and I shall speak for only four or five minutes. But I wish to commend this bill to the attention of the house. I have suggested through the acting leader of the house that the minister might consider this bill on his estimates, so as to save time to-night.
The time has come when judges should be paid properly, and no doubt that will be looked after. But, as is generally known, some judges have been absent from their duties for one or two years. That is not in the interests of the administration of justice, because the frequency with which the judges are drafted for all kinds of such work impairs the efficient administration of justice and causes congestion in the law courts. As they are largely only fact-finding commissions when appointed, they duplicate the efficient powers and functions of parliament, of the committees thereof, and of the many outside boards of recent innovation in war work. Furthermore, they are a costly adjunct to good parliamentary government; they cause delays, and interfere with parliament's right to immediate solution of social and economic problems or urgency to good government. Thus a system of "judicial commission government" is slowly being built up in Canada.
While they are appointed by federal authority they are also provincial officers. No doubt on some commissions they have
Criminal Code

done good work, but I urge on the minister that he should consider this matter in connection with his estimates.
As regards the second section, namely that judges should be bound by the decision of the court of last resort, by the privy council or whatever is the court of final appeal, it reasserts the well known legal doctrine.known as stare decisis, namely that decided cases which lay down a rule of law are authoritive and should be followed. Decisions of the privy council should be binding on all courts. In all the provinces, Quebec excepted, they haye now what they call divorce courts. In my opinion, this jurisdiction in Ontario should be transferred to the county court judges. There were hundreds upon hundreds of cases standing at the York assizes; the list is nearly as long as the clerk's table; I urge that something should be done.
As hon. members know, there is a divided authority between the federal authority and the provinces. The provinces have certain jurisdiction in respect of the solemnization of marriages, an act which is generally performed by the clergy. In one province decisions of the privy council on the marriage law have been upset, and much trouble has been unnecessarily ' caused thereby. It is true that the spiritual bodies represented respectively in the Lambeth conference and the canon law of the province of Quebec are unfavourable to the principles of divorce. Nevertheless, it is there, and one must admit that the way * divorce has been handled throughout the country indicates the need of a change. When all is said and done, it must be remembered that by Roman law marriage was a contract, and a province can pass an act by which such contract can be registered before a mayor, a sheriff, a warden, or a municipal clerk. I do not raise that point in any controversial spirit; no doubt large numbers of people wish to be married by a Christian minister or a minister of some other faith, but I urge that some remedy should be taken along the lines I suggest. If the minister in his estimates will consent to have these two matters discussed at the proper time, I shall be glad to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

FATAL ACCIDENTS AND INjyRIES FROM HIGHWAY TRAFFIC AND LEVEL CROSSINGS
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of bill No. 27, to amend the criminal code (motor cars).
He said: Prior to the last war we used to have a day called "motor accident day".

In 1938 there was a long debate in the house on a motion I introduced with reference to road accidents caused by motor cars. Nothing has contributed more to the education of the people than the motor car, and the proper use of cars is to be commended. But, as in the case of every other invention, its use is one thing and its abuse is another. In the city I come from there were ninety-eight persons killed last year and 7,000 or 8,000 badly injured in consequence of reckless driving. A return was brought down in this house on April 3 giving the number of people killed or injured in traffic accidents on highways during the period of the war, accidents from drowning, accidents at level crossings and so on. Many persons have been killed as a result of fires in small houses and in other ways. In Ontario a member of the forces murdered a girl and was convicted after two trials, but the province spent nearly $70,000 in connection with those two trials. Here we have a record showing 9,038 persons killed and 149,000 badly injured, and no one knows who will be the next victim. There have been some miraculous escapes from the consequences of wild driving at excessive speed contrary to law, but such driving goes on all the year round and apparently no one can stop it.
I would urge the government, when the minister's estimates are up for consideration, to have this matter discussed. There is a real danger from the hit-and-run driver. In the city I come from not a few people have been killed and no one has ever found out who committed the crime. One of our most prominent citizens was killed by a motor car near the York club some years ago and the perpetrator of this dastardly deed was never discovered. It is a cowardly sort of murder, ten times worse than any other. I have seen the headless body of an infant in my constituency, and the people have appealed to me and to one or two other members to see if something cannot be done about it.
I am going to move the adjournment of this debate, but before doing so I suggest to the government that, now the war is over, proper steps be taken to check or to put an end in part to this sort of thing. It takes two persons to make an accident. Reckless drivers wall go past the secondary schools at speeds of from forty to sixty miles an hour in spite of signs warning them to drive slowly. It is the duty of parliament to step in and do something. In New York they have adopted certain modern provisions which I have embodied in this bill. I am suggesting an amendment, the purpose of which is to define the powers of the jury in cases of manslaughter arising out of the operation of

Loan to United Kingdom
motor vehicles, and there is also a section providing that the jury shall decide whether a person charged is guilty or not guilty. It is desirable that the functions of the jury should not be curtailed or abolished. The jury are required to take the law as given by the judge; but, owing to the many cases that are withdrawn by order of the judge, trial by jury in those cases is negatived, and there are at present so many loopholes in our law that many persons guilty of gross negligence get off. The increased number of accidents require that the law with regard to reckless driving should be brought up to date to meet changing conditions, while preserving the liberty of the subject, and there should be a stiffening of the penalties as to drunken and hit-and-run drivers.
I move the adjournment of the debate, and I trust that when the minister's estimates come before the house at the proper time this matter will be disccussed.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for the second reading of bill No. 28, respecting the financial agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom, signed on the sixth day of March, 1946.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
Before this bill is carried there are a number of comments I wish to make on it. With the first feature, the loan of $1,250,000,000 I am heartily in accord. In the light of Britain's extreme and disproportionate war-time sacrifices, most Canadians are pleased and proud to give her a hand with her heavy reconversion and rehabilitation problems. Sentimentally and for humanitarian reasons, I think the proposal has a great deal of merit, and I am inclined to agree with other members who have suggested that the loan would be good business for Canada. I definitely favour this part of the bill.
With regard to the second feature of the bill, however, which proposes to cancel a debt owed to Canada by Great Britain of $425,000,000, I cannot agree. I think that this is tantamount to an outright gift for such an amount. It may be that I am inexperienced in political matters and therefore do not see the problem in the proper light. I am' willing to concede that. I come from British stock and am very proud of the fact; but as a Canadian member of parliament, circumstances being what they are in Canada to-day, I do not see how I can
vote for a gift of such magnitude to another country, even though that country is Great Britain.
In the first place, as nearly as I can ascertain, we have already given Great Britain in the past three or four years, directly or indirectly, over three billion dollars. Over and above these gifts we have sold fann produce to Great Britain in many cases under market levels, and we are still doing so. For instance, wheat on the world market is selling at about $2 a bushel, and yet England is buying wheat at $1.55 f.o.b. Fort William, which means in a nutshell that every time a farmer in western Canada sells a bushel of wheat to Great Britain he is making the mother country a gift of from thirty-five to forty-five cents.
I do not think there are many who begrudge these past gifts, but there are a great many Canadians who are beginning to wonder how long we can fit such vast commitments into our post-war budgets. The war is over and Canada herself faces tremendous problems of reconversion and rehabilitation. Everyone of these projects will require large sums of money.
Everyone admires the magnificent war effort of Britain and is glad to give a helping hand; nevertheless I do not see how we can give away such a huge sum as $425,000,000 when so many of our own people are in actual need.
Only last week there was before this house a resolution urging decent old age pensions for elderly Canadians. Hon. members from all political parties on both sides of the house spoke in favour of that resolution; yet it was not passed. I suppose the reason it was not passed was that the government felt that funds were not available for such social services at the present time. A few days before that, there was before the house another resolution which eventually would have resulted in large_ irrigation projects in western Canada. Despite the fact that these projects are vitally needed, we saw that resolution also talked out, though we heard members from all sides of the house speak in favour of it. I believe it was talked out because the government felt that funds were not available for it at the present time. My home city, of Moose Jaw has a population of almost 25,000 people, and we have been short of water for about forty years. During the past winter our water supply was cut off about half of every day. If a housewife wanted to cook in the daytime she had to fill the bathtub with water the night before. Industries were closed down and men laid off because there was no water. Sanitary facilities could not be used. The people in my constituency will think it strange that parliament can give hundreds of millions of dollars to Great Britain, and yet
Loan to United Kingdom

cannot find a few million dollars to improve living conditions in the cities of Moose Jaw, Regina and Weyburn in southern Saskatchewan. A few million dollars would give them an adequate water supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? I assume he would like to answer his friends in Moose Jaw who are [DOT] worried about this. Would he explain how we can use any part of the $425 million for old age pensions or for any water improvements or for irrigation projects?

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
I cannot tell the Minister of Finance how he should run his department, but I do say this: Surely, if we can find so much money to give Great Britain we can find a few million dollars for that purpose. Probably that is not the answer he would like, but I shall be glad to listen to the minister in a few minutes if he will give me several more. To-day there are thousands of returned veterans who are looking for work. Why cannot we find a few projects on which to employ them? I cannot see how this parliament can justify, on the one hand, being so generous with Great Britain, and, on the other, being so niggardly in many respects to our own people.
I have received no mandate from my constituents to vote for a gift which amounts to about $1,750,000 for every constituency in Canada. I cannot refrain from objecting to this measure, and if the bill comes to a vote in its present form I shall vote against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext: Let us deal with this matter now, because I see the trend of the speeches that are going to be made by certain members and one of the oppositions against this bill.	[DOT]

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext: Just a minute; I do not want the minister to misunderstand. The hon. member for Moose Jaw is speaking entirely for himself in this particular, and I dissociate myself completely froiri the point of view he expressed.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext: That is a mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
Let us deal with that, because I think the hon. member for Moose Jaw wants to be fair about this. I have not given this aspect much thought in advance because I am surprised that that line of argument should be used. H any writing-off of this $425 million will enable us to balance our budget or reduce taxes or pay off any of our debts here in Canada or spend any money on anything that we needed in Canada there would be some validity in the argument.

The capacity of the United Kingdom to pay is limited for the reasons that 1 gave in my speeches to the house. We satisfied ourselves that by the time Great Britain repays the $1,250 million, which will take them until 2000 A.D., it is just nonsense to think about trying to ask them for another $425 million some time in the next century. If we are wrong about our appraisal of Ihe capacity of the United Kingdom to pay, the situation is perhaps a little different; that is, we might get goods of some kind from Great Britain. We could not use the goods to pay old age pensions; nevertheless it would add to the wealth of this country.
The United States made a very careful appraisal of this situation, just as Canada did, and having in mind the fact that the United Kingdom has gone back, as I said this afternoon at six o'clock, by over twenty billion Canadian dollars as a result of this war, and having in mind the fact that we cannot see how Great Britain can meet her deficits-I do not mean her deficits at home, not her budget deficits; I mean her international deficits- how can she pay for the goods that she has to have upon which to live and keep herself going and at the same time even pay interest on the $1,250 million for the first five years, or any more than a low rate of interest for the next half century? What is the use of talking about attempting to collect S425 million? I am taking this in a hard-headed way; I am talking about this as if we had to get it if we could, and I think perhaps that is correct. But bear in mind that this $425 million is a war debt. It was the costs of Great Britain's participation in the air training plan. There is nothing there; it does not represent anything; there is nothing represented by this $4.25 million which enables the United Kingdom to earn a single dollar with which to pay the Dominion of Canada. The reason that we are lending the money to Great Britain as the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar says; perhaps we confuse it by talking money rather than goods-the reason we are sending Great Britain $1,250 million worth of goods or thereabouts during the next three or four years is to get Great Britain on her feet so that she will be a solid, enduring, permanent and expanding market for the Dominion of Canada. This whole deal is an investment in the future of Canadian trade. This deal is for the benefit of these very people about whom the hon. member for Moose Jaw is talking. We are not taking money away from them and giving it to Great Britain. We are now giving money to them as a result of this deal that* we are entering into by this United Kingdom loan.

Loan to United Kingdom
I do not like this arguement that if we can give money to people across the sea, surely we can give more money to people at home. That is not the true nature of the transaction at all. So far as the write-off of the $426 million is concerned, it does not affect one way or the other our ability to do anything along the lines mentioned by the hon. member. I put the question to him a little while ago. I said), if we do not put this loan on the statute books how can we use any part of the $425 million to pay for old age pensions or to pay for Moose Jaw improvements or to pay for irrigation projects in Saskatchewan? How can we do it? There is no answer to that question; there is no way in which we can do it.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
The bill before us is
bill No. 28, respecting the financial agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom signed on the 6th day of March, 1946. This bill has had second reading. Presumably the main principle of it has been approved by a large majority of the house. We are, now in committee of the whole. At this stage I do not propose to repeat the arguments that have been used by any hon. members who have spoken in the previous stages of the bill. I take it that our job at the moment is to deal with the details of the measure.
I have just two or three things to say. I shall sum up the main items in the bill, and state briefly where we stand on it,-although it has been stated before-and to ask the minister to answer a few practical questions relating to it. It will help us all to understand better the implications and the cost of the measure we are now considering.
Let me say this in passing. I conceive this measure to be one of the most far-seeing this government has introduced, in recent years. It is not a measure for to-day or for to-morrow but for the long distant future. I put it in a class with the lend-lease proposals brought forward by the President of the. United States a few years ago, without which the war would not have been won by us. So that I commend the government most highly on the bill. At the same time we must realize that to a considerable degree we are by it making a considerable contribution to an ally in the war.
What is the substance of the bill? It is outlined in sections 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. We are asked to approve the financial agreement entered into some months ago between this country and Britain. To do what? To adVanee $1,250 million to Britain by way of loan, to bear interest after five years at the rate of two per cent; second, to continue for five years more the interest free provisions of the loan
to the United Kingdom made in 1942, which I understand in the beginning amounted) to $700 million and now, I believe, stands at about $500 million. Perhaps the Minister of Finance will tell me if that is right.

speechtext:
Probably you do not

The third provision has to do with the cancellation of the amount owing by the United Kingdom to Canada with respect to the British commonwealth air training plan, totalling $425 million. This is an obligation owing to Canada by Britain which is being written off. Then the government is given power to borrow the amounts of money required for this loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.
We support this bill, Mr. Chairman, chiefly for two reasons. The first is that in our judgment it is essential to the preservation of the Canadian economy as we see it to-day. Ours is an export economy; we are more than any other country dependent upon foreign nations for a market for our products. Three out of every eight people in Canada make their living through enterprises directly or indirectly related to the export business. Our best customer has been Britain. To-day, because of sacrifices made during the war, Britain is unable to pay for the goods she requires from us. As the minister said, this is an investment in trade for the future, to try to keep a good customer going until later on, when she can pay for the imports she will take from us. This measure is essential to the preservation of the Canadian economy. If we lose the British market the farmers will lose a market for a large proportion of what we export. If that should happen we would be in the position of having to let possibly one-third of our Canadian farms be abandoned. We have 30,000 farms abandoned now, and if we have another 250,000 aban-

Loan to United Kingdom

doned, we shall have a job on our hands. If the farmers cannot sell their products they "annot buy the products of industry. Business then becomes demoralized, and we find ourselves with mass unemployment. These things follow one after the other: loss of export markets, demoralization of industry, mass unemployment and a low national income. As the Minister of Justice is reported to have said a few days ago, a low national income means inability to maintain social services at their present standards. These consequences follow one another if we lose a major portion of our export trade. I have said, we support the bill because it is essential to the preservation of the Canadian economy as we know it to-day. It would demoralize our whole economy if the one-third of our people making their living in export industries had to find some other employment in Canada. That is not any sentimental reason for supporting this measure; it is a purely logical, economic reason.
Our second reason for supporting the loan is that it is a necessary prerequisite to the accomplishment of world peace. If we lose our export trade with Britain, Britain will be forced into a sterling bloc, and in this western world we shall have two competing economies, each using the devices of the inter-war period, each sowing the seeds of another war. This is an investment in possible durable peace. These are two important reasons for supporting this measure.
I wish now to ask the minister a number of questions bearing directly on the sections of this bill. What is the understanding or undertaking on the part of Britain that any portion or all of this money will be spent in Canada? My understanding is oiat there is no commitment, but that it is the expectation that an amount equal to the loan will be spent in this country. I should like the minister to make that point clear, for I am sure he would want the Canadian people to be in no duobt about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext: Yes, I will do that.

The United States has made or is contemplating making a loan three times as large. Great Britain will owe on both of them, according to my calculations, $180 million a year. I would like the house and the Canadian people to understand what the obligation is that Great Britain is taking on her shoulders, when taking these two loans. Perhaps the minister has the figure for the United States as well. The interest rate and the terms are exactly the same; only the amounts are different.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946

What is the difference in dollars between our interest payment and the payment we will'receive from Great Britain? The difference between what interest the government will pay us and the payments we receive from Great Britain would be our contribution under that particular section of the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946

But there is a difference. There is a way for the country to lend wealth, as distinguished from the taxpayer paying somebody else in the country. fMr. Bracken.]

The other day the minister gave some reasons why there should be different rates of interest and loans of different lengths to different countries. Perhaps he would dteal with that briefly also.
Why did the government cancel the British debt to Canada of $425 million owing as a result of the commonwealth air training plan? My reason for asking that is this: The United States in its proposed settlement with Great Britain of its lease-lend operations has written off certain amounts which., I believe, approximate $25,000 million, and has asked Britain for payment of only $640 million. We wrote off one debt of $425 million and maintained another of some $500 million. I would suppose the minister's answer will be that he thought Great Britain could pay part of the total, but coyld not .pay all of it.
Those are some of the questions I wished to ask. Speaking for this party, may I state again 63260-591
we are very glad to be able to give the government our unanimous support on this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better answer these questions now. The first one was: What understanding is there that Great Britain, will use the proceeds of this loan for the purpose of purchasing goods in Canada? It is true that it is not provided in this loan that the $1,250 million must be spent in. Canada. It was considered that in the case of Great Britain this restriction was neither necessary nor desirable.
It is not necessary because we know that Britain's purchases in Canada, requiring t.o be financed, by some means other than its current receipts from Canada during the period in which they can use this credit, will exceed substantially the amount of credit. If they use the credit for other purchases, they will need to use other funds for purchasing here, funds derived, for example, from selling to Canada gold or foreign exchange that Canada requires.
It is not desirable because in the agreement, through the operation of article Y, we require the United Kingdom to provide Canadian dollars to countries in the sterling area and to other countries in return for sterling which these countries acquire from their trade with Britain, in order that these other countries may be able to trade with Canada. If we are imposing this obligation on Britain to provide Canadian dollars to other countries which need them for buying in Canada, then we should make it possible for Britain to use the Canadian dollars we lend, her for this purpose.
It should be noted that this will not mean that other countries are getting any special advantage from the credit, but merely that they will be getting the same advantage of convertibility of sterling into Canadian dollars that we wish to obtain by having sterling convertible into United States dollars.
It should also be noted that the credit provided by the United States is not restricted to purchases in the United States and, in fact, it is expected, as Lord Keynes told the House of Lords in England, that only about one-half of the United States credit will be needed to cover Britain's deficit with the United States. We considered that when the United States was prepared to provide Britain with dollars that she can and will transfer to other countries, we should not restrict our credit from being used in this way.
It should be noted that when and if Britain transfers these Canadian dollars we lend her to some other country, the other
Loan to United Kingdom

country in turn will use them in Canada. Our exchange control would prevent these dollars from being converted into foreign exchange and taken out of Canada in this way.
The fact is that we know from the demand for goods during the next three or four years that Great Britain will require more than the amount of this loan for expenditures in Canada. It is different from the United States, because it is not expected in that instance that Great Britain will need the whole amount of the United States loan. Great Britain will need more than the amount of the Canadian loan.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext: What part of the United States loan do you figure she will need?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
I think I have it here somewhere. They would not need the whole amount to meet the deficit with the United States. I do not think I can add much to that explanation.
The second question referred to the circumstances under which interest would be waived. The circumstances are set out in article IV of the agreement. They are a 'little technical and perhaps I had better read that article:
In any year in which the government of the United Kingdom requests the government of Canada to waive the amount of the interest due in the instalment of that year, the government of Canada will grant the waiver if:
(a)	The government of the United Kingdom finds that a waiver is necessary in view of the present and prospective conditions of international exchange and the level of its gold and foreign exchange reserves; and
(b)	The international monetary fund certifies that the income of the United Kingdom from home-produced exports plus its net income from invisible current transactions in its balance of payments was on the average over the five preceding calendar years less than the average annual amount of United Kingdom imports during 1936-38, fixed at 866 million pounds as such figure may be adjusted for changes in the price level of these imports. If waiver is requested for an interest payment prior to that due in 1955, the average income shall be computed for the calendar years from 1950 through the year preceding that in which the request is made; and
(c)	Interest payments due in that year on any credit made available to the government of the United Kingdom to which a similar provision for waiver of interest applies are also waived.
I just want to put in my own language the substance of that article. To begin with, we can waive when the United States waives; the provision is the same as in the United States agreement. We are not obliged to waive unless the United States also waives under the similar provision in their agreement. The simple way to put it is that unless Great Britain's exports, including balances on invisible transactions, are, of a sufficient volume and value to pay for her post-war
[Mr. Ilsley.l
volume of imports, that is to say, imports from 1936 to 1938, we shall consider that Great Britain has not the capacity to pay and we shall waive payment of the interest. That is the simple way to put it and I tried to put it in that way in my speech.
It means that Great Britain's volume of exports must be very considerably greater than before the war. It was stated in the House of Lords' discussion that they must be sixty per cent greater than they were during those years-perhaps it was 1939-during that period before the war. Therefore the United States and this country and Great Britain look forward to an expansion of Great Britain's export trade. There must be a substantial expansion of Great Britain's trade or Great Britain cannot pay for her imports.
How can she pay for her imports? She has a huge population in a small island without many resources. She has lost so many of her investments and her shipping is down, as I said, by about two-thirds. That great volume of investments which she had and which supplied her with large annual payments which she could turn around and use to pay for imports is gone. The result is that Great Britain has to build up a substantial export trade in order to meet the balance of payments. There is just no other way a country -I do not need to go into elementary principles-can pay. A country cannot by taxing its own people get money with which, to pay another nation. In some way or another they have to get reserves; they have to get. the currency of other countries with which to pay other people.

It is generally considered, I think, that the United States interest rate is 1-62 per cent, although the provisions are exactly the same in the two agreements. The effective rate would depend upon the times when the amount was extended, but the best calculation we can make is that the rate will be 1-73 per cent.

I think there are some other questions I have to answer. The next one was, the average rate of interest on our borrowings, the amount that we expect to be paying our own people. The average rate of interest on our outstanding debt is now 2-7 per cent.
On our long-term bonds the yield to-day is only slightly over 2i per cent. speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

speechtext:
Yes, but the Chairman gave me the floor.
I would not have risen at this stage of the debate had my absence from the house last Friday not given rise to some misunderstanding. I was called to Quebec to appear before the superior court, and that is the reason why I could not be here. However, as I owe my constituents a Clear and definite stand on so important a question I should like to say just a few words.
I must state first that if I had been here last Friday I would certainly have voted against the second reading of the bill. Since this measure was announced by the government, even before the beginning of this session, I have endeavoured to find some sound arguments in favour of this bill. Much has been said for and against the bill. I believe that the only true reason for the passing of this measure is found in the speeches delivered by the hon. member for Kootenay-
Loan to United Kingdom

West and by the hon. member for Maeleod. The hon. member for Kootenay-West, as reported at page 847 of Hansard, said:
But I am rising to express support of the bill on the ground that we have a moral obligation to assist those who have suffered in the defence of democracy.
And the hon. member for Maeleod said, as reported at page 848:
The only reason remaining for the loan, as far as I can see, is from the moral aspect.
I believe those statements to be true. I believe that there is much more sentiment than anything else in this transaction, and I say that the government should not have once more tried to side-track the question by endeavouring to show the people that this loan was a good businesslike transaction when everybody knows that it is not so. If it were true that this loan will contribute to maintain our export trade, which is supposed to be vital to our country, one thing which is certain is that this transaction will cost the taxpayers of this country $37,500,000 a year. Furthermore, an arrangement was come to between the Canadian government and the French government which provides for a loan of $242 million with interest at three per cent. I cannot see any reason why the same principle should not apply to the present loan and that interest of at least three per cent should not be charged. We must also keep in mind the fact that the gift of $425 million forms part of our national debt, on which we have to pay three per cent interest, that is to say an amount of $12,750,000 a year. There is also the extension of the loan made in 1942 of $700 million, which, according to figures given by the Minister of Finance, has been reduced to $538 million, which costs us in annual interest $16,140,000. These three figures give a result of $66,390,000 which we are called upon to pay each year to be permitted to sell our products to the United Kingdom.
According to statistics, I understand that nearly one-half of this amount will be paid by those who have an income of less than $2,500 a year. I have in my hand a statement which was given by the government in answer to a question I put on the order paper. The question was, what amount was received by the government during the last five fiscal years from taxes on incomes of $2,500 a year or less; and the answer was-1 take the year 1944-$308 million. I have here a handbook entitled "Canada, 1946", and I see at page 190 that the total tax on incomes for the year 1944 was $756 million. Therefore one must conclude that, of this $66,390,000 already mentioned, those who have an income of $2,500 a year or less will pay, as their share of this

interest, about $30 million a year. I should like to quote from an article written by Mr. P.. M. Richards in Saturday Night of March 23, entitled, "The Cost of the British Loan". This is what he says:
What it's going to cost us-if we dont produce a good deal more efficiently and abundantly than we ever have before-is a part of our "normal" standard of living. Because Britain is not in a position to pay cash for either goods or loan interest at the present time, Canada will pay about $30,000,000 a year in carrying charges on the loan until 1951 and about $12,000,000 a year thereafter the latter being the estimated difference between the two per cent Britain will then pay and the three per cent the loan is expected to cost Canada.
This we may reasonably regard as being by no means an excessive price for the benefits in prospect-the maintenance of British economic health as well as the British market for our products. But, clearly, it does impose a new burden on us, particularly over the next five years when we ourselves will be feeling the strains of social-economic readjustment. We shall bear this burden, now added to all the other burdens (such as family allowances) we have taken upon ourselves, best if we recognize it for what it is and do not make the error of supposing that the cost of carrying it comes from anywhere but our own pockets.
Those are the reasons why I oppose the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
I should like to continue to answer the questions asked by the leader of the opposition. He wanted to know why different rates of interest were charged to different countries and on what principle those rates were fixed. Different rates of interest are charged to different countries under the Export Credits Insurance Act because of the different lengths of the various loans. Our policy is to base the rate on the rate payable by the Canadian government on loans for a period equal to the average period of the credit and to add a very slight margin to cover overhead costs of our borrowing. Of course, this British loan, for the reasons already given, is treated as a special case, and the interest rate has been determined on other grounds. But if the hon. gentleman will look at the rates of interest charged to other countries and the average length of loan to other countries, he will find that they are completely consistent and are based on the rate that the Canadian government pays for money it borrows here.
I have already answered the question as to why we thought it desirable to cancel the $425 million debt. The supplementary question was why we made any distinction between the $425 million debt and the balance of the $700 million 1942 loan. It is just a matter of adjustment. The question is how far a country ought to go. The $700 million loan was a

Loan to United, Kingdom
settled matter covered by an agreement back in 1942 and being slowly but steadily liquidated as securities were sold in Canada; and we thought it desirable to allow that transaction to proceed just as it was doing. We did not begin to charge interest because it did not seem sensible to be asking for interest in the next five years when no interest was being charged on the main loan when capacity to pay was so slight. A similar loan was made in the United States which was not disturbed at the time the loan agreement was made. That is, this loan was secured by what was called a negative pledge of securities. The United States loan was secured by a positive pledge of securities, and that loan is being liquidated by disposition of securities there, while this loan is being liquidated by disposition of securities here. As they did not disturb their pre-existing transaction we did not disturb ours.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946

speechtext: Ours did not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext: No.

speechtext: Two related questions and I am through. Can the minister say what the United States government wrote off in its lend-lease advances to Britain in its adjustment with Britain? The figure I have in mind is 825 billion.

speechtext:
Before I go on with the
remarks which I propose to make, I wish to note one of the arguments brought forward by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay against the measure. He says that we shall have to pay about $30 million a year in taxes if this goes through. Those who believe that the measure will enable Britain to get a better stabilization of the pound and allow us to exchange our credits in England to balance our debits in the United States, think it would be worth while even to pay the $30 million we might have to pay, because it is better to give part of what we shall earn than earn nothing and return to an era of scarcity, which would be the consequence if we lost our British markets. It reminds me of the men who before the war were penniless or unemployed. They received a high salary during the war and were called upon to pay a eftrtain amount in income tax. Some complained bitterly, but others realized that it was better to give part of it than have nothing and be in the position they were before the war. Whether this measure will mean in the end a gift or a loan is quite immaterial. It is the purposes and the results that will count. In some ways
Loan to United Kingdom

it can be considered as a shot in the arm to invigorate Britain and stimulate her world trade, help her to take her place in the industrial life of the world. The purpose is to strengthen the pound and promote a healthy basis of exchange between the dollar area and the sterling area.
The reaction upon Canada is expected to be the balancing of our external trade, which is of vital importance to us. If the British pound becomes exchangeable for dollars we can cover our unfavourable United States balances by our surplus of British pounds; therefore the loan is a necessity to us more than it is to the United States which is granting $3,750 million. The argument has been used before, and I think it is well to repeat it, that we cannot compare the $3,750 million which is the United States share with their wealth on one hand and the $1,250 million and our wealth on the other hand. We should integrate this with the importance attached to our country's export trade. The United States are relying on export trade for between seven and ten per cent of their production, while Canada's economy is counting on an export trade of about fifty per cent.

speechtext:
If it is forty-two per cent, then I am not very far off. This loan will permit us to maintain a productive economy instead of a curtailment economy. To the people of my province as well as to the people of all Canada I sincerely believe it will mean a market for their agricultural products for a good many years to come. It will help to maintain decent prices for the fruits of their labour. Therefore I cannot do other than support the measure even though there are aspects to it which may not be all that we may hope for. I believe this is a necessity. We cannot afford not to make the loan unless we consider the possibilities that remain open to us. As I said a moment ago, unless we grant the loan we shall have a scarcity era, which means that we can produce only for ourselves and our small market outside Britain, or we must take a chance now on building a different type of external trade in the years after the war by diversifying our clients. If we do that, we might dispose during a few years of all our surpluses and' keep the wheels of industry turning by accepting the trade of certain other countries that are clamouring for our goods to-day and are able to pay for them in a way that would enable us to equilibrate our trade deficit with the United States. Can we take that chance of establishing long-
term contracts with such countries and maintain enough of these markets afterwards to replace the loss of the British market? Although I personally think it would be a much saner position for Canada to put herself in, to have a much more diversified external trade, I cannot authoritatively say that it can be easily done.
Our position at present is such a false one in a way that we should try to enlarge considerably our world markets on long-term contracts or by treaties so as not to be permanently in the ridiculous, I might say unsanitary, condition of depending on one client. Any store depending for its success on one client is doomed to failure because it is at the mercy of that client and' must accept his terms. That is the position we are in now because of our trade policies, which were to a certain extent unavoidable at one time. Had we not had the British market we might not have had the onward advance of our Canadian economy. But is it a sanitary condition to be in permanently? I do not think so. I have not given enough study to the possibilities of our building a peace-time market among a number of clients to share with Britain our surplus production in order that we may not be entirely dependent upon one client, to give a definite opinion on the matter. I imagine, however, that the position can be greatly improved. However, it may be that in normal times many of the countries willing to trade with us now may be self- sufficient in most of our sources of export. England has a population of nearly forty-eight millions and cannot feed probably more than ten millions. We have an outright market there. The fact that we have only one client remains unsanitary. But how can we replace that market? Can we find another market for the products that compose our exports? How can we find any place to replace that market? I think we should endeavour to find new markets. Our department of external trade should endeavour to find new markets. However, I believe it would be dangerous to rely on .that at the moment unless we have financial arrangements or engagements with these countries over a long period to come. It would be unwise to turn down the British loan which is our hope-and I sincerely believe it-of balancing our external trade under the same method as we did before the war.
I am sure that, concurrently with maintaining our British market which calls mainly for food products, we should have a more aggressive trade policy with countries that are apt to maintain their payments to us in goods and services or in notes exchangeable

Loan to United Kingdom
on the United States market. Therefore we should meet the present emergency by the loah and try to correct our false position by extending and diversifying our foreign markets. Our industrial production should compete with that of the United States and the United Kingdom in many countries with Which we have an interest to trade.
Let us not have a back-seat to the United Kingdom and the United States in a search for new markets. We have done enough in the last war to deserve to be given now a share of the world markets in order to be able to maintain employment and production at a high peak, but we must go and search for them.
We are in a favoured position compared with formerly industrialized countries like Germany. Let us make the best of it while we can. Another aspect of the British loan is that it is intended to try to restore Britain to its former position in world trade. There are two sentimental reasons to this question. Probably there are other reasons that may be invoked. There are two sentimental reasons for Canada giving this loan. British solidarity appeals to the sympathy of some people because of the sacrifices made in England during the war. I do not think that is a reason sufficient to warrant the loan. We should think of our own interest. Our own interests are enough to warrant it, but I think this is a reason that can be considered. It does enter into the minds of many who support it. I shall not undertake to describe to the committee the conditions I saw when I was over there. I admit I was greatly impressed by what the British people suffered during the war, the ordeal that they have gone through. I saw something of the destruction that has taken place. I learnt something of the sacrifices they made and are still making. That is certainly in the minds of many Canadians at the moment, as probably it was in the minds of those who had to consider this matter. Regardless of how great that sacrifice may have been, I do not think that would be sufficient reason for us to endanger our own economy; but it is a reason that exists just the same.
There is also the necessity of helping Britain to maintain on the continent of Europe the prestige of a democratic nation. I do not want to enter upon a speech on the necessity of counterbalancing the nefarious influences of totalitarian states; far from it. Yet, if we want to show the people of Europe in a certain way that our system of government is good we must make sure that the one country in Europe with a democratic government which stood throughout the war can yet regain its place in international trade, and can still be of great support and great help 63260-60
to many nations on the continent. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, ninety per cent of the population of Europe are underfed or starving. All these people are subjected to subversive propaganda of one sort or another. The only help they can look for is from Britain, the United States and ourselves. We can help in only a small way, but it is worth while to try because it is my personal belief that you cannot fight the propaganda which is being spread among, those people who have nothing to eat just with nice words and empty hands.
I believe we have to give them something; we have to give them confidence, and start them on their way to trade. I think Britain, with the help the United States and Canada are giving, is bound to regain, to at least some extent, the position she occupied before the last war in connection with trade on the continent of Europe.
One argument brought forward by sympathizers with Britain, in favour of the measure, is that it will certainly help Britain to regain her lost supremacy in world trade. Personally I think this is an illusion. Britain gained her industrial supremacy during the eighteenth century, when the invention of the steam engine gave her a chance to use her vast coal resources. Britain thus got an advance as well as an advantage over other nations. With the advent of electrical power and the needs of modern industry for oil, Britain had lost her industrial lead before the first great war. She remained the money market of the world up to the beginning of the second war, but the drain on her financial resources has been such as to change Britain from a creditor to a debtor nation. She came out of the war with a debit balance, we are told, of $13,000 million; not counting the $3,000 million of Canadian aid and the $29,000 million of United States lend-lease. Is it possible that these present advances of $5,000 million can permit her, as we hope, to regain her balance and get on the way to recovery? I sincerely hope so, but without being a prophet of doom I think it will be just a shot in the arm. I may be wrong; I hope I am, but even after having reached that conclusion it is not sufficient to deter me from supporting the bill, because I think we must take the chance that it will have the expected result. That is my first reason for supporting the bill.
In the second place, no matter how wrong I think it is to depend upon one client, I think we must face the facts as they are and must help Britain stabilize the pound sterling in order that we may equilibrate our world trade balances by using, to pay for our excess imports from the United States, the payments received for our excess exports to Britain.

In the third place I think it is better to lose the yearly interest on our money for five years and then the difference between the borrowing rate and the rate paid by Britain, than to reduce our industrial activities and curtail our production. It is better to have ahead of us what I might call a period of artificial prosperity than, a period of depression; and even if this should prove to be a gift, as some people have said, because of the possibility of Britain's inability to meet her obligations, I think it is better for our economy in the next few years to go ahead with the measure just the same. I repeat, however, that it is high time we considered means to restore to Canada saner methods of external trade than that of the one client system. We should now gain new markets for our industrial production. In the past we have been exporters of raw materials and wheat. During the war we became a highly industrialized country, turning out ships, planes, tanks and heavy equipment. Let us carry our industrial recovery into the peace era and better equilibrate our external trade by seizing new markets for our industrial products. It is imperative that we do so unless we want our industrial and economic fate to be tied indefinitely to that of Britain. Canada is a young nation. She must look ahead for new fields to conquer. Let us not be limited by sentimentalism or a false method of world trade.
I am far from being enthusiastic about burdening the Canadian people with more charges, and I would not consider sentimental reasons only as sufficient to warrant this measure. It is not with pleasure that I see this provision for the cancellation of the British debt to our country, which is estimated in the present bill at $425 million. But if we consider the aim and purpose desirable; if we consider that it is imperative for the benefit of our Canadian economy to see Britain resuming her capacity to trade with the world, and if we consider it desirable to strengthen and support her currency in relation to the United States dollar, then we have no recourse but to cancel the debt, and I think the minister made the point quite clear a moment ago.
In short, I think in our present position we cannot act differently from the United States at the present time, and we must try to help British recovery, not only or not even because she deserves it on account of her contribution to the freedom of the world, but because in our present position a measure of British recovery is an economic necessity for the welfare of our own country.
